This research also provides upper limits on the fraction of dark matter comprised by ultra-light axion-like particles, concluding that, as a single species, such a particle cannot constitute more than 10% of the dark matter in a given mass range ($10^{-21} < \mu \, (\mathrm{eV}) < 10^{-17}$).

Creating intelligent, neuroinspired systems poses a significant challenge due to its underlying hardware complexities. To overcome these challenges, a thorough comprehension of its fundamental building blocks is essential, coupled with the development of straightforward and user-friendly prototyping tools. To address this issue, an open-source emulator was designed, allowing users to model the functionality of advanced neuromorphic systems with ease. This emulator, written in Python, accurately simulates analog circuit dynamics while providing a lightweight, non-specialized framework. As a result, users can rapidly design, test, and refine their system's hardware components, encompassing digital logic and communication layers. The emulator's capabilities were demonstrated by successfully reproducing the dynamics of a cutting-edge neuromorphic chip and by emulating the system components of a large-scale, neuroinspired computing system.

A solar type-I noise storm is created by particle beams accelerated from active regions experiencing significant changes in their magnetic field configurations. These storms exhibit significant intensity fluctuations in very short time frames and on very short wavelengths. The dynamic evolution of these storm sources remains largely unstudied due to a lack of high-resolution imaging data in metrewave frequencies. By analyzing data from the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA), this research identifies a new aspect of these storm sources associated with minor flares. It reveals the existence of two distinct modes of co-evolution: a "sausage" mode, in which storm intensity decreases while size increases, and a "torsional" mode, in which storm size changes correlate with sky-orientation changes. The researchers have also developed the capability to precisely localise these storm entities and track their movement over time, thereby gaining new insights into their behavior. The results of this research will be useful for future monitoring and analysis of these storm entities and their relationship with microflares.

A compact magneto-optical trap has been successfully developed, using a planar-integrated design that merges an optical grating chip and a magnetic coil chip. This novel setup minimizes the size and weight of the trap, requiring only a single laser beam to capture a population of approximately 10,000 cold rubidium atoms. The improved MOT architecture reduces the distance between the optical and magnetic components, allowing for easier integration and a smaller overall design. This integration strategy and the utilization of a single integrated circuit offer potential advantages in scalable optical trapping.

The spherically symmetric merging of a kinetic cloud of particles onto a Schwarzschild black hole is investigated. Unlike earlier research, which established boundary conditions at a distant point, we examine this process with properties of the cloud specified within a finite sphere of radius. We use a series of models, ranging from simple to complex, to study how mass accretion onto the black hole changes over time. Our models are based on a well-known equation that describes the interaction between a dissipative fluid and gravity, and we anticipate the mass accretion rate to be influenced by conserved angular momentum within the cloud. Our models are solved numerically and we analyze their behavior by evaluating properties such as radial and angular momentum transport, as well as changes in radial momentum and internal energy within small volume elements of the cloud. We find that models which respect angular momentum results in lower mass accretion rates compared to models without angular momentum. Our work has potential applications in understanding the merging of stars and black holes in compact binary mergers.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror.

A longstanding issue regarding massive star origins involves whether these stars always form within dense clusters and, if found in less crowded environments, can they be newly formed or have migrated there.  Two key pieces of evidence supporting extratropical massive star origins include those from the recently-discovered large magellanic cloud (MMC 01, MMC 02) and ngc 1929.  Both were found based on radio sky surveys, yet their ages and cluster associations are unknown.  We present multi-wavelength observations of these stars, consisting of broad band spectroscopy, optical spectrometry, radio spectral mapping, and near-infrared imaging, which provide evidence that these stars are indeed young and likely reside in recently-forming star clusters.  Our data imply that these stars are relatively newly created and have not yet moved from their birth location, thus supporting theoretical ideas that massive stars can develop outside of dense clusters and aligns with recent findings from radio sky surveys of massive stars.

Degraded handwritten documents, which are susceptible to damage from paper ageing and environmental factors, can cause severe readability issues for current text recognition algorithms. To overcome these challenges, we propose an innovative, end-to-end approach utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks that not only restores visual clarity but also improves the overall readability of the documents. This pioneering method differs from conventional binarization techniques, which primarily focus on enhancing visual quality, by integrating a text recognition module to optimize generated output. The effectiveness of this architecture was validated through comprehensive experiments conducted on Arabic and Latin handwritten texts, showcasing improved readability and visual quality. Additionally, our pre-trained model demonstrated exceptional performance on the H-DIBCO challenges, even after fine-tuning on synthetic, degraded text images.

The growth of Information Technology has significantly influenced information sharing, but it has also raised concerns about data privacy. Obtaining and processing physical documents is costly and time-consuming. Document image scanning is a labor-intensive process, whereas OCR software can facilitate faster conversion of images to text, ultimately enhancing data processing efficiency. But traditional OCR may struggle with formatted or structured documents, necessitating more advanced techniques like Tesseract OCR. Nevertheless, Tesseract OCR has limitations in handling ID card layouts, necessitating the integration of Layout Analysis. This study introduces an end-to-end solution using a combination of Tesseract OCR and Layout Analysis, specifically with an ID card template, to improve extraction accuracy of text from ID cards. This approach was tested with an ID card from South Africa and yielded a character-level extraction accuracy of 99.89%, with character-level correction accuracy of 99.98%, and word-level correction accuracy of 99.71%.

In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable channel estimation vital for optimal system performance, yet the IEEE 802.11p standard's limited pilots lead to inadequate channel tracking. As a result, conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators experience significant performance decline, particularly in high-speed scenarios. To overcome these challenges, researchers have explored deep learning (DL) techniques for channel estimation in IEEE 802.11p. Notably, a considerable majority of related studies have concentrated their simulations in static scenarios, disregarding the complexities of high-speed environments. Conversely, this work proposes a novel two-stage solution consisting of a SLAM-based simulator, utilizing simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), to address fast-changing environments; and a convolutional neural network (CNN), to enhance estimators' performance, specifically in rapidly changing high-speed scenarios. The proposed solution is rigorously evaluated within a comprehensive framework of scenarios, encompassing a range of common fixed and mobile channels.

The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community for a limited time. Colorization is particularly challenging due to its inherently high degrees of freedom; where multiple color combinations can achieve a similar visual outcome, making it difficult for machine learning algorithms to pinpoint a singular result. Although deep neural network-based approaches have been applied to this task, they often require an extensive dataset of paired images to facilitate learning. The availability and creation of such large image collections, however, pose significant practical challenges. In response, a novel approach to colorization is presented, where a generative adversarial network is conditioned on an image's style representation, which is derived from its embedded features. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance when compared to previous research on single-image colorization and achieves comparable results to state-of-the-art techniques requiring paired images.

We've developed a novel numerical scheme to efficiently calculate Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) weights without relying on tedious iterative processes. Based on the Universal Approximation Theorem, our proposed algorithm rapidly achieves low error rates in the regression and classification of intricate datasets, such as the Griewank function and the MNIST database for handwritten digits. Its mathematical formulation allows it to accurately approximate highly complex nonlinear functions with a minimal margin of error, and it also facilitates the solution of Partial Differential Equations. The approach works by determining the weights for each neuron in localized data subsets where a corresponding approximation matrix remains invertible, thereby rendering hyperparameter optimization unnecessary. As a direct consequence, this minimizes computational speed. With respect to observations, our method requires no replications. Additionally, the algorithm's computational cost is directly proportional to the number of observations. Furthermore, the proposed scheme exhibits stability and exhibits a smooth and stable behavior in the training phase. It should be noted that while certain issues with non-invertible approximation matrices may give the impression of oscillations in weight values, these are purely artificial and do not affect the accuracy of the neural network. Conversely, poor performance may arise from an insufficient number of data points. Nonetheless, increasing the data set size has been shown to consistently yield high accuracy rates in our experiments.

The Early Career Researcher panel was established by the European Committee for Future Accelerators to gather input from young researchers at universities and research centers. The panel recently conducted a survey of its members, focusing on how early career researchers can be best supported within the European research community. This paper presents the findings of the survey in relation to career development needs and suggests concrete actions for the ECFA and its members.

Confining modes propagate along an infinitesimally thin interface separating two custom-designed electromagnetic surfaces, where one is engineered for dual responses in frequency and orientation, and the other is a standard ground plane. When the gap between the surfaces becomes negligible, they can be represented as an effective boundary that supports a unique type of wave - the line wave. This new type of electromagnetic wave has never been observed before, and it follows a specific set of equations that describe how the wave propagates, including a unique relationship between electric and magnetic fields. To understand the origins and applications of line waves, we developed a comprehensive theoretical framework and performed three experiments, where we used specialized techniques to visualize the wave, developed new ways to control it, and successfully harnessed its unique properties for enhanced wireless communication and detection.

One of the most effective approaches to building intelligent robotic systems is Learning from Demonstration (LfD), however research is still needed to overcome challenges such as multi-agent learning and prolonged autonomy.  A new architecture for multi-agent LfD is introduced which enables the creation of reliable and efficient robotic systems in complex and large-scale environments by leveraging advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) through the implementation of a Federated Learning (FL)-based collaborative learning environment involving both humans and robots. This novel approach capitalizes on local edge computing and AI-driven processes at multiple robotic platforms to generate a unified, AI-driven global model that is shared across the network, and utilizes human-robot interaction instances to inform learning. This innovative framework extends the traditional LfD approach to encompass multi-agent settings, incorporates human learning within existing robotic frameworks, and incorporates advanced AI methodologies to model interdependencies between robotic tasks, and it demonstrates its applicability through the implementation of a realistic industrial case study in a dynamic agile production system that recovers critical raw materials.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing the problem of irregularity that typically hinders conventional bias correction.  To overcome this limitation, a specific alternative strategy was implemented.  Establishing the bias correction of the estimator involved proving non-zero pathologies at edges of the parameter space.  Constructive methods were used to address these issues.  A key aspect was addressing the non-smooth nature of the model and its resulting impact on bias correction.  A simulation study was conducted to evaluate the performance of the new bias-corrected estimator.  Additionally, the method was applied to real-data sets to analyze its practical implications.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating the original object should also be included in the
list. In our study, we utilized this connection by implementing a multi-task
approach, training existing relation extraction models alongside knowledge graph
link prediction to ultimately boost the models' overall performance and achieve
predictable gains in accuracy.

The Analytical Exact Iteration Method has been employed to solve the N-dimensional Radial Schrödinger equation for bound states, with particular focus on bound quarkonia, and the outcomes have been contrasted with the Variational Method. By doing so, the dissociation temperatures for various quarkonium states as a function of anisotropy in the N-dimensional context can be determined analytically, which is not the case when utilizing the Variational Method. Interestingly, anisotropy was discovered to decrease the dissociation temperature below the isotropic mark. Furthermore, the approach accurately captures the anisotropic ground state up to the relativistic correction order without requiring the introduction of an effective mass. Results for the Kaon and Dion ground states, including their dissociation temperatures in the N=3 dimensional space, were also output.

Our study focused on the magnetic arrangements within the crystals of Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 using neutron-diffraction experiments. In Tb3RuO7, neighboring ruthenium atoms created a chain pattern, with some being ordered magnetically and others remaining randomly aligned. This unique combination resulted in an intermediate disordered state, with the two ruthenium types exhibiting similar yet distinct behaviors. In Nd3RuO7, the magnetic patterns were uniform and independent for the two ruthenium species, with both being ordered at temperatures below 17.5 K. We attribute the disordered state in Tb3RuO7 primarily to the magnetic frustrations, caused by the differing internal magnetic fields imposed by the ordered terbium atoms on the two ruthenium species, leading to distinct behaviors.

Multi-Layer Perceptrons are primarily understood as a straightforward,
computer-readable representation of neural networks that lacks the
complexity of actual biological neurons. Despite this simplicity, MLPs
have shown exceptional performance in numerous image and video
classification tasks when enhanced with autoencoding and other unsupervised
techniques. However, these modifications come at the cost of complicating
the MLP architecture. To simplify signal representation and take advantage
of the expressiveness of MLPs, we introduce an innovative dual-MLP
structure for autoencoding images and videos. By dividing the input
signal into two parts and processing each with a separate MLP, we have
observed significant improvements in both the expressiveness and
trainability of our model. When evaluating our model through
cross-correlation analysis, we found that one MLP is capable of encoding
low-frequency components, while the other processes high-frequency
features. Notably, our model demonstrates superior performance when
evaluated on various image and video classification datasets.

Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data for either determining importance weights or density estimates. Then, a model is trained using only labelled data. We're examining a special instance of covariate shift that also enables learning from unlabelled data, effectively merging adaptation with semi-supervised learning techniques. By drawing on causality concepts, we propose a novel method that requires equal amounts of unlabelled and labelled data. This method is based on finding a shared latent variable. We've designed experiments to demonstrate the feasibility of this approach and conducted analyses to validate its reliability. Results from these experiments suggest that this new method is capable of accurate density recovery and provides reliable importance weights. Moreover, it offers superior performance compared to SSLL and DSL methods. This means that using unlabelled data during adaptation does indeed enhance performance.

Despite its impressive task execution capabilities, the inner workings of deep learning systems remain shrouded in theoretical uncertainty. In the study of deep learning, geometric models play a vital role in uncovering these uncertainties. This research contributes to the development of geometric frameworks by demonstrating the geometric connections underlying various deep learning architectures. Specifically, the study reveals geometric structures in neural networks, such as Lie groups and algebras, and shows how different neural network types correspond to distinct geometric models. The study also explores the implications of these geometric structures on the performance of deep learning models. The findings of the research may facilitate the design of new deep learning architectures informed by geometric principles. In the near future, the study suggests potential applications of geometric structures in enhancing the performance and robustness of deep learning systems.

We consider the field extension $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d},\zeta_3)/\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_3)$ where $\zeta_3$ is a primitive cube root of unity and $d$ is a positive cube-free integer. Our work examines the behavior of the chain of lattice minima in the cubic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d})$ arising from the prime factorization of $d$ in relation to generators of ambiguous principal ideals. Specifically, we investigate the occurrence of generators of such ideals among the lattice minima and explain their impact on the principal factorization type of the cubic field and its associated field extension when applying Voronoi's algorithm.

A research framework is introduced to uncover and analyze decision-making processes from deep neural network classifiers. To achieve this, the study uses a novel method, known as DREB (Deciphering Rationale by Exciting Bases), which incorporates an initial network that detects critical features, and a second network that generates binary explanations. By applying DREB to a renowned jet substructure tagging technique, the study finds that network explanations consistently surpass the official predictions when evaluated on an independent test set. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that expert variables, representing jet substructure components, significantly contribute to the model's performance. By integrating DREB into the training process, the study demonstrates that expert variables can be learned more efficiently. Interestingly, the results show that leveraging expert variables within DREB improves performance, and training with the extracted explanations enhances model reliability.

For every positive integer r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into a specified number of non-empty subsets, where each subset contains at least r elements. We're introducing a variation of these Stirling numbers, which represents their extreme forms, reducing to well-known cases when r equals one. This paper seeks to establish formulas linking these variations together.

Eighty sets of layer groups were examined, each consisting of four types: ordinary and double, as well as gray single and double. Layer group properties allowed for the efficient computation of relevant physical characteristics using symbolic methods, thanks to code such as POLSym. This involved an initial step of categorizing irreducible domains based on their action within the Brillouin zone and the topology of the torus. Additionally, band representations stemming from site symmetry groups were broken down into irreducible components. This theoretical data on layer group symmetry was then tabulated and made accessible online.

Momentum operators are explored within the context of intrinsically curved manifolds. A key discovery indicates that for all s, the momentum operator corresponds to a simple, symmetric tensor that aligns with Levi-Civita connection on manifolds, regardless of their curvature type. When the manifold is of the compact type, the momentum operator will always have a positive definite, holomorphic curvature. This research further clarifies the characteristics of momentum operators on specifically designed manifolds: those with constant sectional curvature and hyperbolic manifolds: (i) on constant sectional curvature manifolds, s = 2; (ii) on hyperbolic manifolds, s, n, and λ must be in a specific, non-degenerate relationship.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem.

In a composite Higgs model, where $SU(6)/Sp(6)$ is used, the flavor symmetry is identified as an $U(1)$ subgroup of $Sp(6)$. Here, the complex scalar field's', acting as a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson, plays the role of a flavon, which bears a flavor charge. Upon the VEV of the flavon, $U(1)_F$ flavor symmetry is broken. This break results in the emergence of a small parameter and consequently generates a hierarchy between top and bottom quark masses. A flavon lighter than the TeV scale can naturally be introduced, which makes it a completely testable model to understand the flavor hierarchy origins. Furthermore, its effect on the substantial flavor-changing neutral currents arises and gets constrained heavily by flavor precision experiments. Research into the direct search for additional scalar bosons is conducted using HL-LHC and upcoming hadron colliders.

The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations, like redirected walking and haptics, extends VR interaction beyond conventional physical limitations by exploiting the boundaries of human perception, subtly guiding users' movements to enhance interactivity. This research examines the dangers of VPPM exploitation, beginning with a conceptual framework that confirms their existence and then applying speculative design to identify and mitigate threats. Through practical examples, we demonstrate how current VPPM practices can inadvertently create vulnerabilities that may lead to physical harm. This study seeks to highlight the potential consequences of VPPM applications and dissemination as they stand today.

To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains.

Recent high-resolution observations using VLA and CARMA telescopes have unveiled previously unknown details of proto-stars in binary systems. Specifically, mass measurements obtained from chemistry and dynamical analysis reveal significantly greater masses for the star formation process than previously expected. Utilizing numerical simulations, this study validates that more massive binary fragments are produced when the parent core's mass and angular momentum are high. Furthermore, variations in binary mass are primarily influenced by core mass, while changes in orbital distance are mainly affected by fragmentation depth. In more massive cores, binary stars tend to form farther apart due to a faster fragmentation process, resulting in greater separation. This prediction can be tested through future observations to better understand the process of star formation.

This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with ICA to overcome the limitations of previous methods. Although the kernel trick offers a powerful way to tackle non-linearity, its effectiveness can be undermined by a lack of open-source and reproducible kernel implementations, especially in complex datasets. The proposed m-ar-K-FastICA approach uses a readily available and adaptable Python library that facilitates collaboration with scikit-learn, providing a more reliable solution for feature extraction even in data sets with high entropy levels and no need for data normalization. The reliability of the m-ar-K-FastICA method was verified by symmetric matrix creation, extreme case testing, and its efficiency in comparison to alternative methods was demonstrated with the use of artificial and real-life data sets.

This paper builds on existing research linking finite model theory to algebraic and propositional proof systems. It's proven that if a logic system can identify unique, non-isomorphic graphs in a specific category, then a related proof system can do so as well, under certain conditions. This allows researchers to apply existing findings about the latter system to the former, shedding new light on CPT's limitations. Establishing a polynomial CPT lower bound via a related PTIME-instance could resolve a long-standing question in finite model theory. Additionally, the findings provide a theoretical explanation for the separation between polynomial calculus and extended polynomial calculus within bounded-degree settings.

A subring collection in a ring $R$, that is associative, commutative nor unital, is defined as proper subrings set-theoretic union equating $R$. If such a collection exists, the smallest possible number of subrings in the collection is denoted as the covering number and is represented as $\sigma(R)$. In this research paper, the focus is on determining the covering numbers for specific types of rings as well as providing general theorems on upper and lower bounds for infinite diagonal rings $R_x,y$. Additionally, relationships between covering numbers and ring properties including upper bounds based on ring width and the presence of non-zero nilpotent elements are investigated.

Social media platforms host an immense volume of content, encompassing a broad array of views on society. Despite the numerous opinions expressed, verifying their accuracy can be challenging due to their subjective nature. To address this, we aim to condense these posts into distinct narratives, thereby isolating the core claims associated with each. By using DeBiT, a system designed to identify recurring themes (narratives) within an online dataset, we can trustworthily isolate the central claims related to each, allowing for the assessment of their accuracy. DeBiT achieves this by employing a combination of machine learning and human evaluation to distinguish genuine narratives from artificial ones, thereby establishing trustworthiness as a key factor in building its models. We rely on existing annotated datasets to create multiple model variations, each addressing a separate challenge in post-processing social media content. Our system was found to perform satisfactorily in two separate evaluation exercises, one comparing its performance with other existing approaches and another testing its relevance in real-world applications, by outdoing other systems in both scenarios.

Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographical locations is crucial, particularly for anticipating incidents such as accidents, protests, or breaking news. The dynamic nature of social media data poses challenges to traditional approaches, including ambiguous event timelines and spaces. An innovative solution, this research introduces an adaptive spatio-temporal event detection framework leveraging social media. The framework incorporates three key components: a data preprocessing module, an event resolution module, and a data visualization module. The former ensures accurate data analysis, the second aggregates social media posts by event, and the third illustrates recognized events. The framework was tested on 100 hours of social media data from locations such as New York and London and was successfully used to identify multiple events over extended periods. The framework's efficiency and effectiveness make it a suitable solution for real-time social media event detection across various locations.

New, high-precision data from the cosmic microwave background lensing measurement by the Planck mission and non-local gravity tests are presented in this study. Initially, a novel weighted skew-spectrum technique based on CMB temperature and E-mode polarization is developed to optimize the extraction of information on large-scale structure growth. This method showcases enhanced sensitivity to the combination of primordial power spectrum and non-GR effects when comparing counts of overdensity and tomographic maps. Through multiple datasets, including galaxy clustering from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and Cloussey, as well as measurements of baryon acoustic oscillation from the SDSS and WiggleZ, it's found that current constraints on Gpc-scale new physics still allow for ambiguity in possible gravity models, with GP parameter GPchar approximately equal to 3.4+/- 1.9, and further data will be needed to conclusively decide the gravity question. Next, we investigate the potential of future surveys by the SDSS and LSST to constrain gravitational models, finding that the proposed Phase 31.1 and Phase IV surveys of the SDSS will be able to rule out non-GR models at a 95% confidence level if the galaxy sample extends to z equal to 2.5, while the LSST's yBand dataset will be able to tightly constrain GPchar. Finally, we discover that the predicted sensitivity of future surveys to the growth rate of structure, characterized by f sigma 8, will be within reach, with

By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we developed a rigorous framework for training certifiable Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). This approach combines constraint relaxation and modified cross-entropy loss to achieve robustness to potential attacks. The method, demonstrated through empirical tests on standard datasets, allows for training BNNs that are both accurate and securely invariant to malicious perturbations. Specifically, our results show that this approach can be used to train BNNs that are formally certified as being free from Trojan horse attacks on the CIFAR-10 dataset. This achievement represents a significant advancement in the field, as it allows for the creation of BNNs that are both reliable and securely invariant to malicious perturbations, thereby addressing key challenges in the development of deep learning algorithms.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this, we identified several popular tracking platforms and aggregated data from BingMaps to pinpoint areas experiencing high anxiety levels. Subsequently, we applied our proposed method to analyze repeated outbreaks of the same rumor within these areas and found that our algorithm successfully pinpointed areas experiencing high anxiety levels on multiple instances, also detecting new areas on certain occasions.

This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks. Five methods (PCA, KPCA, ICA, AE, and DAE) are utilized to compress high-dimensional pixels down to 301 dimensions. The resulting pixels are used for classification, allowing a comprehensive assessment of each method's effectiveness based on classification accuracy, compression rates, and the influence of feature selection on dimensionality reduction. Our research reveals that more aggressive compression rates lead to lower classification scores, highlighting the trade-offs between computational efficiency and classification performance caused by dimensionality reduction. Additionally, our data indicates that simple linear techniques (like PCA) often surpass more complex non-linear methods (like ICA), contradicting some common hyperspectral imaging practices. Our findings also suggest that excluding irrelevant pixels can improve classification performance across all compression rates, and that some modes of dimensionality reduction (like KPCA) are less susceptible to noise and outliers than others (like ICA).

Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within various layers is complicated, resulting in the networks often being referred to as 'black boxes.' In contrast, simpler models are more interpretable but they are also much harder to find. Identifying and utilizing a sparse network that can be trained to replicate the same results is a viable option to improve network interpretability. According to the lottery ticket hypothesis, even large, dense neural networks harbor a smaller sparse sub-network that can be trained independently to achieve the same accuracy in the same amount of time. Our objective is to explore the existence of this trainable sub-network within the realm of natural language models, and we will accomplish this by examining and evaluating the most recent model compression techniques, such as quantization, knowledge distillation, and pruning.

A novel prediction method, referred to as ProCS, enables fast and precise calculation of crucial chemical shift indicators in proteins, thereby determining the spatial arrangements of proteins. ProCS is calibrated with the results of high-level quantum mechanical calculations, achieving remarkable agreement in predicting the amide proton chemical shifts of a small protein with a minimal error margin of 0.25 ppm (high correlation coefficient of 0.94). ProCS is now compatible with the PHAISTOS protein simulation program and used to determine ensembles of proteins representing experimentally measured amide proton chemical shift values. The ProCS method is used to refine the structures of proteins G, ubiquitin, and SMN Tudor Domain from high-resolution X-ray structures to align their predicted and experimentally measured properties. This study reveals that quantum-mechanical-based predictions of chemical shifts are essential for optimizing protein structures to align them with the observed data. ProCS presents an innovative tool for optimizing protein structural arrangements with immense potential in studying various biological processes like the conformational flexibility in ligand binding interactions.

The choice of loss function for a neural network being trained from scratch under supervised classification tasks warrants closer examination. While the cross-entropy loss is widely adopted, our research indicates that certain other loss functions can yield superior performance, especially when the number of classes is substantial. The key insight lies in their ability to impose stricter data augmentation incompatibilities during training, which can translate to improved out-of-distribution detection capabilities. The finding is validated through extensive experiments on various datasets, including those like ImageNet and CIFAR-10, and further substantiated by analysis of how the incompatibilities affect the generated neurons.

Describing the behaviors of complex systems comprised of strongly interacting elements requires concise expressions for their internal relationships. Ensuring the stability of these systems is the primary focus. Parquet theory is capable of achieving a level of self-consistency that encompasses all strictly pair-based interactions among elements. Grounded in a perturbative framework, the theory is comprised of a series of nonlinear integral equations that describe scattering events at all levels, constrained by principles of symmetry but also inherently heuristic. Within the context of a theoretical framework developed by Kraichnan, a new Hamiltonian-based analysis is applied to parquet's structure in the context of fermionic particles, resulting in a natural formation of the theory's underlying equations through its canonical representation. This approach reveals the inherent connection between the conserving properties of the derived scattering amplitude and the traditional parquet theory. Although the derived amplitude conserves properties at a microscopic level, it does not maintain symmetry. In contrast, the traditional amplitude maintains symmetry but fails to ensure conservation at any point. Ultimately, the decision to use one amplitude over the other is determined by the specific requirements of the system under consideration rather than its adherence to a theoretical ideal.

The process of exciton condensation leads to the spontaneous creation of electron-hole pairs and triggers a phase transition in a semimetal that forms an excitonic insulator by creating a common ground state for these pairs. This phenomenon presents an intriguing model for particle condensation that can be studied through experimental research and theoretical analysis. A novel approach to investigating exciton condensation involves analyzing a related model that retains key characteristics, the Hubbard model, which has a well-established understanding of its behavior under various conditions. By studying how the parameters of this model affect its behavior, researchers can gain new insights into both the Hubbard model and exciton condensation.

In the US, various safety organizations have adopted text-based systems for processing community members' incident reports, which necessitated a need for system extension to include emotional support features for these individuals. Through observation and literature review, it was noticed that standard multi-agent system architecture, which relies on natural language processing for emotion detection, may not always work effectively, particularly in communities having limited digital access. Therefore, a new extended MAS architecture was proposed, which was later implemented using Java to guide the development of a prototype. Which was subsequently implemented using Java in the EmoS system, which was then tested and validated through a survey of 11 organization providers, yielding positive outcomes. Results indicated the potential for MAS systems to learn from their environments and display empathy when responding to community members' incidents.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response in the presence of a magnetic field, particularly exhibiting edge effects that are absent when the superconducting and topological properties are uniformly distributed throughout the sample. Conversely, when the external magnetization is solely driven by a superconducting vorticity, the resulting chiral superconducting state exhibits distinct characteristics that distinguish it from its nematic counterpart, notably characterized by a specific ratio of magnetic response components. This research provides valuable insights into the inherent characteristics of superconducting topological insulators like Bi$_2$Se$_3$.

Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods are susceptible to outliers and diversity-based methods may overlook key information. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised active learning approach that simultaneously considers both uncertainty and diversity in a minimax framework. Our method incorporates a network that minimizes entropy and an entropy-maximizing classifier, while a discriminator is trained to distinguish labeled and unlabeled data. We then select the samples with the highest entropy that the discriminator identifies as unlabeled for human annotation. Experimental evaluation on image classification and semantic segmentation datasets demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

To study how music changed over time, we measured the structure of songs by
calculating their variability in intensity, duration, and melody characteristics.
Using a large, pre-labeled dataset of songs spanning six decades, from the
1960s to the 2010s, spanning various genres including pop, rock, and hip-hop,
we analyzed the distribution of these structural elements and found that song
complexity generally decreased over time, despite an increase in the number
of sub-generes during this period. Notably, the most popular songs tended to have
lower complexity and more consistent melody patterns than less popular ones.

A novel category of stochastic processes that incorporate reinforcement involves sequences of random groupings denoted as $\{\mathcal{P}_t\}_{t \ge 1}$. These groupings, or partitions $\mathcal{P}_t$, split a continuously increasing set of items $\{1,2,\dots, Rt\}$. When time progresses to $t$, a fixed number of items $R$ are appended to this set; a fraction of these added items joins existing groups based on probabilities defined across different time intervals, initiating new subgroups separately for each $t$. These stochastic processes, which include the Galton-Watson tree random branching processes as a fundamental sub-class, exhibit complex symmetry where the probability distributions governing each $t$ are inherent to the process yet unpredictable from one $t$ to another. Our research focuses on establishing an exact expression for the expected size of each group $\mathcal{B} \in \mathcal{P}_t$, denoted as $\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{B}]$. Our approach to derive this expectation employs a complex expression involving the stochastic process's fundamental characteristic function. Ultimately, our research reveals that attempting to predict the future growth probability distributions of this process's groups from one time point to another is destined to fail, a phenomenon we refer to as 'temporal unpredictability'.

Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that the inversion principle embodies the notion of harmony itself, while the recovery principle serves only to ensure harmony is preserved under expansion of judgements. Additionally, this paper demonstrates how to derive the harmony condition from a more fundamental property, the cut-elimination theorem, by employing a method similar to that used in computational types.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. To effectively use these partial labels, we divide the learning process into two stages: initially, we train a contrastive predictor to generate a minimal and structured set of environmental states, and subsequently, we employ these simplified states in a standard Q-learning routine. Our approach was verified by achieving a notable improvement when using our label efficiency technique, as demonstrated in both simulated environments and a real-world robotic experiment.

We show that a topological space's Smyth powerspace is core-compact if and only if the original space has local compactness. Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties.

We're investigating singular vorticities in ideal two-dimensional fluids with specific properties derived from point vortices and vortex sheets. These characteristics are embodied in "pointed vortex loops," allowing us to concentrate on their corresponding orbits under area-preserving diffeomorphisms on the 2D real plane. The results show that a specific subgroup within these diffeomorphisms preserves the shape of the vortex loop itself, indicating the configuration space is comprised of loops confining a fixed area regardless of the vorticity distribution and any connected points.

The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a causal parameter that can be estimated in two steps, initially modeling treatment and outcome to incorporate potential confounders, then applying predictions to ATE estimators, such as AIPW, with potential alternatives being Machine Learning algorithms due to their non-parametric nature and capability to handle complex relationships. In order to improve the efficiency of two NN models with no parameter regularization except SGD, our simulations indicate the significant drawbacks that arise when AIPW is used. In an effort to improve this, the proposed nAIPW offers the same double robustness and orthogonality as AIPW and can achieve asymptotic normality under specific conditions. Additionally, when imposing L1 regularization on the first step NN models with convergence, nAIPW and AIPW are evaluated based on their bias and variance.

The role of $\tau$ is taking center stage in the current research into lepton flavor universality violations in B-physics, warranting greater theoretical attention in new physics models. Enhanced $\tau$-mediated interactions, stemming from its smaller Yukawa coupling, increases the likelihood of detecting new physics effects. A specific, well-motivated model - the optimized vector-boson exchange model - is examined here. For each possible signature involving hadron or leptonic decays, global optimisation is employed to determine the most effective new physics scenarios, taking into account experimental constraints. A final likelihood analysis is applied to determine the most preferred values of new physics scales.

A tabletop-sized rotating annulus setup has been extensively studied to mimic the characteristics of large-scale atmospheric circulation patterns, particularly those that facilitate cyclogenesis. Our experiment leverages the analytical insights derived from simplified atmospheric circulation models to frame the study. We examine the relationship between two key factors, differential heating and friction, under which stable, unstable, and neutral conditions are investigated, followed by the analysis of the formation of vortex Rossby waves and their role in cyclogenesis. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms involved in the formation of storms in atmospheric circulation systems.

A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter'm'. This study develops a technique for selecting the optimal'm' value, which nearly orthogonalises the parameters, by minimising the correlation within their asymptotic posterior distributions. By choosing this optimal'm', the parameters converge faster and efficient sampling is possible using Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. Finally, parameter values are then extracted through a straightforward transformation. We present results from simulations involving models of both identical and non-identical extreme rainfall in Cumbria, UK.

In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adversarial robustness, a critical consideration in RL that deals with the challenge of learning a nearly optimal policy when a fraction of data tuples may be compromised by a malicious adversary. Our study begins by examining a worst-case scenario in which an adversary can alter the training dataset through any means, and finding the minimum fraction of adversarial influence that can impede an agent's ability to learn an optimal policy. Our analysis reveals that even under the restrictive condition of only modifying the next state in the transition tuple, it's estimated that approximately $1/nc^2$ fraction of adversarial influence can obstruct an agent's ability to learn an optimal policy for some value of $n$ and $c$. This finding underscores the significance of developing methods that prioritize robustness in offline RL, and we respond by proposing a robust learning framework based on the concept of counterfactual reward estimation. Our proposed approach achieves optimal reward convergence in theory and demonstrates robustness in the presence of adversarial manipulation, and we evaluate its empirical effectiveness using various levels of adversary influence.

This study demonstrates a logarithmic convexity linked to observability at a specific point in time for a one-dimensional heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions, leading to impulse approximate controllability in similar scenarios with dynamic boundaries. Additionally, we provide a detailed estimate for the cost of impulse control. Our research includes a step-by-step procedure for finding the impulsive control of minimal L^2-norm and supports these findings with numerical tests to verify the efficiency of the developed algorithm.

A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified two primary strategies, model calibration and density estimation, for identifying data points that fall outside predetermined datasets and examined their performance across various distribution shifts. "Nearest-neighbor" density estimation methods exhibited greater resilience to background shift and mixed shift scenarios, whereas model calibration performed better in background shift scenarios. Nonetheless, a challenge in relying on density estimation lies in its vulnerability to sparse background data, rendering it ineffective in such cases. Consequently, incorporating a mix of density estimation and model calibration might provide a more comprehensive approach for identifying out-of-distribution examples.

In recent years, various artificial molecular motors utilizing electric currents have been explored, and like Brownian machines, they generate directional rotation from random tunneling events. Despite their potential to drive molecular machines of the future, their theoretical modeling is understudied. Here, we create a mathematical model to describe their operation by forming a density matrix that accounts for the interaction between motor molecules and their surrounding electric fields. The model's predictions are validated by comparing experimental results with data obtained from density matrix calculations. The findings reveal that both experimental and theoretical approaches converge to similar outcomes. Furthermore, we identify potential research directions, and demonstrate that utilizing spin-polarized scanning tunneling spectroscopy could provide valuable insights into molecular motor operation.

Building on a 2014 framework, researchers introduced various interpretations of transducer behavior, some differing significantly from traditional understandings. In this study, further insights into close approximations between two-way and one-way transducer models were gained. Specifically, we demonstrate the possibility of determining whether a non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be transformed into an equivalent one-way model, with a solution existing for any given transducer. Notably, this is a problem that cannot be generally solved. By establishing a simplified method for evaluating a transducer's one-way equivalence, we can now also determine if a two-way transducer has an equivalent one-way form. Additionally, we provide a solution for determining if a transducer replicates a given word under specific reading conditions. These results do not apply to origin semantics, where other complexity issues exist.

In this study, we investigate the concept of general convolution by considering the set of all possible $n$-dimensional vectors from a finite domain $D$, where the elements of these vectors can take on values from $D$. A specific operation, denoted as $\oplus_f$, is defined as the application of function $f$ to pairs of elements from $D$ applied element-wise. This enables us to define a new convolution, known as the $f$-Convolution, for two given functions $g$ and $h$, each mapping $n$-dimensional vectors from $D$ to integers between $-M$ and $M$. Upper and lower bounds on the complexity of computing this $f$-Convolution by brute-force are derived as $\Theta(M^2|D|^2)$, where $|D|$ represents the size of domain $D$. Additionally, we demonstrate how a more straightforward approach can achieve a time complexity of $\Theta(M|D|)$ under more restrictive conditions, such as when $f$ is a simple addition function. These findings on the $f$-Convolution are closely related to a recent publication by Braverman, Iglesias, and Panconesi, where a more general problem was addressed, involving the interaction of multiple functions applied to pairs of elements, which yields a more complex bound of $\Theta(M^2\cdot |D|^2 \cdot \log^2 |D|)$.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, yet a detailed analysis with current spectroscopic methods has been lacking, especially concerning its atmospheric features, which display unusual properties and contradict earlier estimates of the dwarf's mass and orbit, requiring further examination due to their implications for intermediate population object formation processes. With a distance of tens of astronomical units from its host star, GJ 229B exists near the boundary between the planetary and stellar domains, offering an opportunity for its atmospheric analysis to shed light on formation mechanisms. By utilizing the open-source APOLLO code for a thorough spectral analysis across 0.5-5.1 ${\rm \mu m}$, we derived a precise mass estimate of $41.6\pm3.3\, M_J$ and an accurate temperature assessment of $869_{-7}^{+5}$ K that corresponds with evolutionary models, indicating the system to be older than 1 billion years, and also identified high CO molecular abundance replicating earlier observations, which provide implications for this object's formation and evolution, further contributing to the knowledge of analyzing brown dwarfs and planets through new-generation telescopes.

To resolve the long-standing uncertainty in the experimental data, the status of exotic states containing $s$ quarks has been reviewed. Assuming the current assumptions are correct, the analysis suggests there's sufficient evidence to suggest the potential existence of a unique, unusual $D_s^{*}$ resonance below 2 GeV, weighing around 2.49 GeV. However, the existence of the $D_s^{(*)}$ resonances observed in the $DS^+ K^0$ mass spectrum, and the $D_s^{\pm}$ events detected by the LHCb, remains uncertain and requires further clarification. The review also discusses the conventional charmed states containing $s$ quarks observed through various decay processes, and the potential for exotic states containing $s$ quarks to be discovered at future facilities such as the Electron-Ion Collider, or in new experiments focusing on $\tau$ decays.

A crucial goal of the LHCb experiment is to establish the $C\!P$-violating phase $\phi_{s}$ and decay width difference $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ caused by $\bar{b}\to\bar{c}c\bar{s}$ decays. The precise prediction of $\phi_{s}$ within the Standard Model makes it a favorable means for detecting signs of new physics. The experiment's $\phi_{s}$ and $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ measurements are discussed in detail, encompassing the 2011-2012 data set of 3.0~fb$^{-1}$. Future analyses are expected to contribute significantly through the incorporation of additional results derived from decay modes with reduced branching fractions.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, exhaled breath, sneezed droplets, and infected individuals' location, even before considering the absorption of particles. We use numerical models for double and three-dimensional airflow to investigate the movement of virus-carrying aerosols. In simplified scenarios, we simulate various phenomena such as breath and coughing, passenger distribution, and bus layout to analyze the capture process of aerosols. These simulations reveal the complex aerosol dynamics and offer insights that can be applied to evaluate the transmission risk on buses.

This study has conducted large-scale shell-model computations for $\beta$-decay attributes. Researchers at ILL, Grenoble, recently performed $\beta$-delayed $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy to investigate $\beta$-decay properties related to the transition of $^{137}$Te ($7/2^-$) to $^{137}$I with various final $J$-values. We conducted a comprehensive shell-model analysis of nuclear properties and compared our results to experimental findings. We then reported our computed $\beta$-decay attributes, such as the $\log ft$ values and the mean shape factors. Our study marks the first theoretical calculation for $\log ft$ values in conjunction with these novel experimental data. Additionally, we also calculated the $\log ft$ results for $^{135}$Te ($7/2^-$) decaying into $^{135}$I with different $J$-values.

Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching of demand and supply. Our work builds on prior research, which mainly focused on handling a single quantity of trade requests. To expand this knowledge, we developed methods to support multiple quantity trade requests and established fully formalized matching algorithms for double-sided auctions. These algorithms come with rigorous correctness proofs. Additionally, we formulated new notions of price consistency for double-sided auctions and provided a characterization of our first-fit declining order strategy in terms of bid and ask price fairness. To demonstrate the practical value of our research, we conducted an experimental evaluation of our matching algorithms and established a formal proof of safety and liveness for our double-sided auction system using the verified algorithm tool, fstar. To further enhance the reliability of our research, we also developed a new notion of price instability and provided the first evidence that our double-sided auction system remains free from price manipulation. To facilitate the implementation of double-sided auctions in practical settings, we provided a verified implementation of a central system and a decentralized alternative.

We utilized heavy quark effective theory to investigate the $F$-wave bottom mesons, applying both theoretical and experimental data to calculate the mass of these mesons. Additionally, by examining the decay widths of bottom mesons, we derived upper limits on their corresponding coupling values. Our research further included constructing Regge trajectories in the planes of angular momentum (J) and squared mass (M^2), yielding predictions that align neatly with Regge theory lines. These outcomes may hold significant implications for future experimental research on this topic.
Michal Szabados initially proposed this research in his PhD dissertation. It includes all necessary authorizations as outlined in the thesis.

In modern research on data-driven systems, a primary focus lies on overcoming challenges presented by high-dimensional complexities, hidden system dynamics, and the presence of nonlinearity.  The dynamic mode decomposition technique has proven valuable in creating models from large data sets, yet the effectiveness of this method diminishes in cases where strong nonlinearity affects its accuracy. Conversely, sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics is able to learn comprehensive models, differentiating between linear and nonlinear interactions; however, it is limited in its application to lower dimensional systems. We introduce a kernel-based approach to generating dynamic mode decomposition to address the issue of strong nonlinearity in large data sets. Our method is founded on the principles of two-manifold learning and can be applied to systems both with and without a physical basis. We show through multiple examples, including the simulation of a turbulent flow and real-world data on the dynamics of a laser, that our approach yields accurate models, differentiating between linear and nonlinear interactions, and producing results comparable to those of sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics.

The timeless appeal of chess persists, with its strategic intricacies still captivating players across the globe, particularly when it comes to mastering the intricacies of Opening Theory, which requires extensive knowledge and years of dedicated study. Our innovative approach harnesses the collective wisdom of online chess enthusiasts to provide insights previously reserved for expert chess players. Firstly, we establish a chess opening network that evaluates the similarities between different opening strategies. This helps us identify clusters of commonly used openings and their connections, insights not easily extracted from existing classification systems. Additionally, our model successfully forecasts future opening preferences and verifies these predictions against actual results, demonstrating superior accuracy over random forecasting. Lastly, by utilizing an advanced algorithm, we assess the level of difficulty for different openings and the skills required to execute them proficiently. This groundbreaking study not only transforms our understanding of chess analysis but also makes possible the use of network analysis to provide individualized suggestions for players, helping them improve their gameplay with data-driven opening recommendations.

This research explores the observational characteristics of millisecond pulsars in terms of their magnetic fields, rotational periods, and masses. Our analysis is grounded in the concept of accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs within binary star systems, enabling a more nuanced comprehension of millisecond pulsar demographics. Moreover, our findings underscore the significant evolutionary linkage between neutron stars and white dwarfs within stellar binary systems, particularly through the process of accretion-induced collapse.

A method to derive constants of motion beyond local bounds for ODE-based Lagrangian systems is outlined, including a practical example that illustrates its utility for dissipative mechanical systems and its implications on solution existence and behavior under specific assumptions. The framework is further extended to cover Euler-Lagrange equations with order greater than two, yielding new first integrals for particular models, such as the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator, paving the way for potential applications in Euler-Lagrange partial differential equations in the future.

Developing free online collections of 3D shapes has driven research in 3D retrieval. Debates surrounding the optimal input method for retrieval and the ultimate application have been ongoing. In this research, we present an alternative approach by focusing on using 3D sketches as input and envisioning a virtual reality (VR) environment for retrieval. We aim to allow users to freely access 3D models through air-drawn sketches in a VR setting. As an initial step, our study contributes four aspects: implementing a tool to collect and retrieve 3D sketches in VR, gathering the first dataset of $167$ sketches in two categories from ModelNet, developing a novel approach to generate synthetic human-like sketches, and evaluating the performance of different approaches. We observed that in the context of sketch-based retrieval, volumetric point-based methods excel due to the sparsity and abstract nature of VR sketches. We believe our work will serve as a foundation for future studies, and the associated VR interface, code, and datasets can be found at https://tinyurl.com/3DSketch3DV.

HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a significant 1000-fold increase in the heat it receives due to its highly eccentric 64-day orbit. As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps dramatically from 400K to 1400K in a matter of hours during its closest approach. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon take advantage of this planet's extraordinary environment to study various aspects of its atmosphere. Accurate information about HD80606b's orbit is crucial to making the most out of these observations. Researchers have studied the planet's transit orbit using a novel technique and have discovered slight irregularities in its 64-day and 10.5-day periods, as well as evidence of other, undetermined patterns. These findings are consistent with current understanding and do not require the presence of any other planets. As a result of these discoveries, predictions for the planet's transit and closest approach may need to be revised in the next decade.

In this investigation, we're looking at how a specific type of matter collapse, governed by a certain relationship between pressure and density, behaves in a certain type of gravitational system. The effect of this relationship on the dynamics of collapse is significant. It's found that this relationship leads to a situation where the equations that govern the collapse can't always be solved consistently. We've found a boundary beyond which the equations can't be solved. In order to understand the behavior of collapse more accurately, we've replaced the original relationship with another one that's more physically sound. The effect of this change on the dynamics of collapse is also explored.

Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we have developed a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the extremality bounds and entropy of Kerr-Newman black holes following any arbitrary perturbation. This method involves integrating an effective stress tensor and shows, under certain conditions, the correction is equivalent to the standard stress tensor, thereby illuminating the relationship between extremality corrections and energy conditions. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that to lower the mass of an extremal black hole in a canonical ensemble as stipulated by the weak gravity conjecture, the perturbation must breach the dominant energy condition. We have successfully applied this method to compute higher-order corrections to black holes in anti-de Sitter space and to Kerr black holes.

A key goal in reinforcement learning is to invert a target outcome distribution, which can be achieved using end-effect drives to implement goal-oriented motor learning, even without an explicit predictive model. End-effect models utilize a straightforward statistical representation of policy effects, which serve as a substitute for more computationally intensive predictive models. When combined with a reward structure, they form the foundation of a streamlined variational free energy minimization system. However, the primary challenge is balancing the upkeep of this simplified effect model with the constant changes in policy and environment. Interestingly, the optimal balance between these competing demands can be represented by an unconventional measure - the amount of surprise generated by ending the episode. In this study, we illustrate how our framework addresses the challenge of inverting a target distribution within a complex environment, which is both numerically and empirically demonstrated.

A generalized three-dimensional Poincaré algebra has been developed that incorporates colour symmetry. This enhanced algebra can serve as a basis for modelling coloured Poincaré gravity and exploring generalised models of massive and massless free particles in three dimensions. Multiple generalised particle models have been presented, which distinguish themselves in terms of the coloured Poincaré orbits they describe. Our methodology provides a potential pathway to describing particles in non-abelian backgrounds and serves as a starting point for the worldline formulation of an associated quantum field theory.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs.

Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring local
self-guidance throughout a journey to a destination. Previous models often
utilize a separate memory system for image navigation, but generally fail to
utilize their primary model memory, despite it being potentially beneficial.
Our proposed model, MemoNav, incorporates a novel type of short-term memory
known as the Episode Memory (EM), designed to enhance navigation by storing
episodic experiences consisting of multiple visual images. The EM maintains
a visual representation of each episode, similar to a slide show, with
intermittent image presentation. During navigation, each episode is presented
with new images, with the goal of estimating the destination's probable
appearance when the episode ends. Our model is available at
https://github.com/simrom1/MemoNav.

To increase cellular capacity, operators initially implemented 4G LTE small cells (Femto Cells) by augmenting existing licensed spectrum. However, these cells' capabilities sometimes exceeded the licensed spectrum bandwidth. As a result, operators engaged in unlicensed spectrum use, particularly in the 5 GHz Wi-Fi band, for their 4G LTE small cells in areas with low infrastructure. Consequently, there is a need to investigate the optimal coexistence of Wi-Fi and 4G LTE small cells operating in the same frequency band. This study proposes an innovative coexistence technique of 4G LTE small cells and Wi-Fi access points, allowing them to dynamically adjust their transmission power to maximize each technology's performance. A practical algorithm was developed to implement this technique, leveraging only available standard tools, and was then evaluated through simulations using 3GPP and IEEE standards. The outcome of these experiments showed that this method can effectively optimize 4G LTE small cell and Wi-Fi performance while ensuring stable coexistence.

We've developed a comprehensive framework to model complex interactions between multiple entangled systems using hypergraphs. This approach can be applied to several processes and we'll specifically explore how certain conditions lead to spontaneous pattern emergence in systems where individual units interact with each other. Our focus will be on two specific settings: one involving interactions between groups over long distances, and another with diffusive interactions between units. Additionally, we'll demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through applications to both the generalized Volterra system and the Brusselator model.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis.

The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state consisting of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, has been a topic of interest for a long time. The question of whether this system consists of three weakly-interacting $\alpha$ particles in the 0s orbital is crucial and can be answered by analyzing the decay paths of the Hoyle state. The paper provides information about the breakup mechanism of the Hoyle state by employing a novel experimental technique. The investigation of the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay of the Hoyle state, rather than through the $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$ ground state, can be performed through an advanced analysis of the energy distribution of the three $\alpha$ particles from the decay. Using beta-delayed charged-particle spectroscopy, the relative importance of these decay paths can be quantified. Additionally, the study allows for the verification of the assumed structure of the final 3 $\alpha$ system, which is necessary for evaluating the decay amplitude for the Hoyle state decaying directly to three $\alpha$ particles. The outcome of the investigation provides significant insights into the structure of the Hoyle state and its potential as an $\alpha$-condensate.

Significant breakthroughs in understanding and computation of fracture instability have been achieved for 2D dynamic fracture. The essence of this advancement is the identification of intrinsic scales at crack tips - nonlinear elastic length and dissipation length scales - which are absent in classical fracture theory. Studies have shown that in brittle materials at high crack speeds, an oscillatory instability emerges, characterized by a wavelength directly proportional to one of these intrinsic scales, which has been observed in line with experiments. Through phase-field fracture models, we find the following features of this oscillatory instability: (i) It also exists in materials with linear elastic behavior near the crack, depending solely on dissipation properties; (ii) It undergoes a type of supercritical bifurcation; and (iii) It's minimally affected by factors like the fracture energy associated with a certain dissipation time. These results support the idea that this oscillatory instability is an inherent feature of fast cracks in 2D, while we also show that an ultra-high speed instability can be attributed to a limiting rate of energy transport near the crack. The numerical framework of the fracture approach used in this study is thoroughly described.

In a general setting, we examine the properties of finite state channels equipped with feedback and state information, which becomes available to the encoder in a predictable sequence. This encompasses a broad range of channels, including memoryless channels with independent and identically distributed states (referred to as the Shannon strategy), channels with Markovian states that offer the ability to access past states (known as look-ahead access) and energy harvesting. The capacity of these channels with feedback is described in terms of the directed information between auxiliary variables and the channel outputs.
